# Broadside gunnery and the line of battle (`naval_gunnery_line_of_battle`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs cannon_artillery; helped by ship_design_caravel_carrack, blast_furnace_cast_iron, ballistics_gunnery
- Core idea: Heavy guns on wheeled truck carriages stand on the lower decks of a strong sailing ship and fire through hinged ports cut in the side, low down so the ship stays stable. Because nearly all the guns point sideways, a fleet fights in a single line ahead, each ship following the next, so that every broadside bears and no ship masks another. This turns the ship from a platform for boarders into a floating battery and lets a few hundred men defeat much larger forces on galleys or junks, which is what carried European power overseas.
- Pitfalls:
  - Gunports close to the waterline left open in a turn; the Mary Rose (1545) and Vasa (1628) sank that way
  - Heavy guns high up capsize the ship
  - The rigid line avoids defeat but rarely gives decisive victory; that needed breaking the enemy's line (1782, 1805)
  - Guns are useless without trained crews and standard shot that fits
- History: europe: c. 1500 – lidded gunports (the usual credit to Descharges of Brest, 1501, is unverified); 1502 – Portuguese squadron fights in line off Malabar; 1588 – Armada campaign fought with guns, not boarding; 1653 – English Fighting Instructions order the line ahead; 1805 – Trafalgar; east_asia: 1592 – Yi Sun-sin's cannon-armed Korean fleet defeats Japanese boarding tactics; china: 1520s – Ming copy Portuguese breech-loading ship guns (folangji); islamic: 1571 – Lepanto, galleys with bow guns; 17th c. – Ottomans build sailing warships; india: 1509 – Diu, Portuguese gunned ships defeat a Mamluk-Gujarati fleet
- Read:
  - N. A. M. Rodger, The Command of the Ocean: A Naval History of Britain 1649–1815 (2004)
  - Carlo M. Cipolla, Guns and Sails in the Early Phase of European Expansion, 1400–1700 (1965)
  - John F. Guilmartin, Gunpowder and Galleys (1974)
